evidence_quotes.quote: Poisson regression models were used to test the statistical signiﬁcance of monthly, yearly, and seasonal peaks in the DWA time series data.
Characteristics of the drinking water systems in which the DWAs were issued were summarized using tables and descriptive statistics.
Across all 402 DWAs reported, almost half (47%) occurred in drinking water systems where the primary operator did not have adequate training for the treatment system (See Table 3).

printed_headline_estimate: N = 402 drinking water advisories (DWAs) in Ontario First Nations community water systems (2004–2013): Poisson regression tests of temporal/seasonal peaks report p < 0.05 only (no regression coefficients, SEs, or CIs printed) for annual peaks in 2011 (15% of DWAs, p < 0.05) and 2013 (75 DWAs, 19%, p < 0.05; p. 6, Fig. 2), July count = 52 (12.94%, p < 0.05 vs. January reference count = 19, 4.73%; Table 2, p. 7), and Summer count = 129 (32.09%, p < 0.05) and Fall count = 107 (26.62%, p < 0.05) vs. Winter reference count = 76 (18.91%; Table 2, p. 7). System/operator-training characteristics (Table 3, pp. 7–8) are descriptive counts/percentages among DWAs only.
publication_year_note: Published 17 May 2016 in Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 2016, Vol. 13, Issue 5, Article 505 (Received: 8 February 2016; Accepted: 20 April 2016; Published: 17 May 2016).
rationale: The full text is a cross-sectional descriptive and time-series analysis of 402 drinking water advisories (DWAs) issued in Ontario First Nations community water systems from 2004 to 2013. While the paper conducts inferential Poisson regression models (p. 5–7, Table 2), those models exclusively test calendar-time and seasonal variation (year, month, and season peaks relative to the lowest-count year, January, and winter) within First Nations community systems—failing narrow Criterion 2 because no legal, regulatory, governance, tenure, tariff, or institutional exposure is tested inferentially. All water system attributes (including primary operator training adequacy in Table 3, pp. 7–8) are presented solely as descriptive counts and percentages among issued DWAs without a non-advisory or non-First-Nations comparison group or inferential test, and the discussion of fragmented federal on-reserve water governance and regulatory gaps (pp. 9–10) is purely qualitative.
